pages.text: Every spring evening, the lamps came on in the square. And every evening, the drummer came too. He sat on the steps with his big round drum.
pages.speech: Every spring evening, the lamps came on in the square. And every evening, the drummer came too. He sat on the steps with his big round drum.

pages.text: Children ran to sit around him. Tala sat right at the front. Her mum sat on a bench nearby. Pigeons walked between their feet, pecking at crumbs.

pages.text: “Tonight we’ll play a game,” said the drummer. “I drum a word. You guess it.” He looked at the wall, where a cat was dozing. Boom.

pages.text: “Cat!” shouted a boy. “Yes,” said the drummer. “Cat has one beat.” Then he looked down at the pigeons. Boom-boom.

pages.text: “Pigeon!” shouted Tala. Pi-geon: two beats. The drummer nodded and smiled. Then the pigeons flapped up into the air, all at once.

pages.text: Next the drummer played a long one. Boom-boom-boom-boom. Four beats. The children looked at each other. Nobody knew.

pages.text: The drummer pointed at the fruit cart in the corner. “Watermelon!” the children shouted. They clapped it together: wa-ter-mel-on. Four claps.

pages.text: Then the drummer looked straight at Tala. Everyone went quiet. He drummed very, very softly. Boom-boom. Two beats.
pages.speech: Then the drummer looked straight at Tala. Everyone went quiet. He drummed very, very softly. Boom-boom. Two beats.

pages.text: Pigeon? thought Tala. No, the pigeons had flown away. Two beats… and he was looking at her. Can you guess the word?
pages.speech: Pigeon? thought Tala. No, the pigeons had flown away. Two beats… and he was looking at her. Can you guess the word?

pages.text: “Ta-la,” she shouted. “It’s my name!” The drummer laughed and drummed it again, softly. Boom-boom. Ta-la.
pages.speech: “Ta-la,” she shouted. “It’s my name!” The drummer laughed and drummed it again, softly. Boom-boom. Ta-la.

pages.text: Everyone clapped Tala’s name together. Ta-la, Ta-la. Then they clapped their own names too. Some names had one beat. Some had two, or three.
pages.speech: Everyone clapped Tala’s name together. Ta-la, Ta-la. Then they clapped their own names too. Some names had one beat. Some had two, or three.

pages.text: Tala walked home with her mum under the street lamps. She clapped everything she saw. “Lamp.” One clap. “Win-dow.” Two claps. At her door, she clapped one last word. “Home.”

activity.title: The Name Drum
activity.goal: Compare which word is longer by counting its beats.
materials: A pot or a plastic bowl

steps.caption: Turn the pot over. Drum your name.
Drum every name in the family.
Whose name has the most beats?

activity.safety: Use an empty, cold pot that has not been on the stove, or a plastic bowl. Drum gently, and only on the pot. If there is an accident, call your local emergency number.
activity.forAdult: In the story, Tala finds out that words have beats, and that her own name has two. Hearing the beats (syllables) in a word is one of the first steps towards reading. Turn a pot upside down on the floor and start yourself: drum your own name, one beat for each part. For example, Dad has one beat, Grand-ma has two and ba-na-na has three. Then the child drums their own name and the names of everyone at home. Ask: “Whose name has the most beats? Whose has the fewest?” To see the difference, lay out a spoon for each beat, in a row. Say the names slowly and naturally. In families with two languages, the same name may have a different number of beats in each one. Ten to fifteen minutes is enough. To make it easier, clap instead of drumming. To make it harder, drum a word for the child to guess, like the drummer in the story.
activity.inClass: Sit in a circle with one drum (an upturned pot or a box). The adult starts by drumming a child’s name without saying it. The group guesses whose name it is, and that child becomes the next drummer. Names with the same number of beats make good riddles: the group may need two or three guesses.
